VOLUNTEER VS. EMPLOYEE CLASSIFICATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Charitable Foundation

VOLUNTEER ROLE DECLARATION
Volunteer: Jordan Lee
Organization: Acme Charitable Foundation
Supervisor/Coordinator: Taylor Morgan
Volunteer service dates: October 1, 2026 through December 31, 2026
Typical hours per week: 5

The following statements describe this volunteer arrangement as structured by Acme Charitable Foundation. They are factual statements about this specific arrangement, not a legal conclusion about Jordan Lee's status under the Fair Labor Standards Act or any state wage-and-hour law.

Organization type: ☐ Nonprofit or charitable organization  ☐ Public agency (government employer)  ☐ For-profit business  ☐ Other (describe): _______________________________________________

Compensation: ☐ Jordan Lee does not expect, and will not receive, any wage, salary, or cash compensation for this service  ☐ Jordan Lee will receive payment or compensation (describe): _______________________________________________

Nominal benefits or reimbursement, if any (for example: mileage or expense reimbursement, meals, a uniform allowance, or a small per-shift stipend): _______________________________________________

Voluntariness: ☐ Jordan Lee's decision to provide this service was made freely, without pressure, coercion, or the threat of any adverse consequence  ☐ Other (describe): _______________________________________________

Relationship to paid work: ☐ Jordan Lee is not otherwise employed for pay by Acme Charitable Foundation to perform the same type of services described in this declaration  ☐ Jordan Lee is otherwise employed for pay by Acme Charitable Foundation, and the services described in this declaration are of a different type than Jordan Lee's paid work  ☐ Other (describe): _______________________________________________

Nature of the activity: ☐ This service is of the kind commonly understood as civic, charitable, humanitarian, or religious volunteer work  ☐ Other (describe): _______________________________________________

Description of duties: _______________________________________________

THE FLSA'S BROAD "EMPLOY" DEFINITION AND THE JUDICIALLY RECOGNIZED VOLUNTEER EXCEPTION
The Fair Labor Standards Act defines "employ" very broadly. The statute itself states only that '"Employ" includes to suffer or permit to work.' That text, standing alone, says nothing about volunteers and states no exception for unpaid civic, charitable, or humanitarian service. The exception for genuine volunteers comes not from this statutory language but from judicial interpretation. In a 1947 decision addressing unpaid railroad trainees, the Supreme Court held that this "suffer or permit to work" language "was obviously not intended to stamp all persons as employees who, without any express or implied compensation agreement, might work for their own advantage on the premises of another," and that the Act's broad definitions do not sweep in "each person who, without promise or expectation of compensation, but solely for his personal purpose or pleasure, worked in activities carried on by other persons either for their pleasure or profit." The Department of Labor has applied this same reasoning specifically to unpaid volunteers, including in the private nonprofit and charitable sector. Separately, federal regulations at 29 C.F.R. Part 553 define "volunteer" and address volunteer compensation in detail, but by that Part's own terms those regulations govern only public agencies — state and local government employers — not private employers, whether nonprofit or for-profit. This document did not locate a Department of Labor regulation of comparable specificity governing private-sector or nonprofit-sector volunteers; their status instead continues to be assessed under the judicially developed doctrine described here together with related sub-regulatory DOL guidance discussed elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The definition “suffer or permit to work” was obviously not intended to stamp all persons as employees who, without any express or implied compensation agreement, might work for their own advantage on the premises of another."
  — Walling v. Portland Terminal Co. (CourtListener text), 330 U.S. 148, 151-52 (1947) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/104376/walling-v-portland-terminal-co/)
  "without promise or expectation of compensation, but solely for his personal purpose or pleasure, worked in activities carried on by other persons either for their pleasure or profit"
  — Walling v. Portland Terminal Co. (CourtListener text), 330 U.S. 148, 152 (1947) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/104376/walling-v-portland-terminal-co/)
  "“Employ” includes to suffer or permit to work."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 203(g) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Fair Labor Standards Act, definition of "employ" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/203)
  Known gap: This clause describes a general judicial doctrine; it does not itself determine that any particular unpaid arrangement is, or is not, genuine volunteering. The 1947 case quoted here concerned unpaid trainees, not volunteers at a nonprofit or charitable organization as such, and predates the modern nonprofit-sector case law discussed in a separate clause in this document; this document does not claim that case addressed nonprofit volunteering directly, only that later authorities have relied on its reasoning in that context.

CONSIDERATIONS DISTINGUISHING A VOLUNTEER FROM AN EMPLOYEE
Beyond the basic requirement that a genuine volunteer not expect or receive compensation, DOL guidance and case law examine further considerations. One is whether the service was offered freely, without pressure or coercion — federal regulations describe this as central to Congress's intent "to prevent any manipulation or abuse of minimum wage or overtime requirements through coercion or undue pressure upon individuals to 'volunteer' their services," and state that "[i]ndividuals shall be considered volunteers only where their services are offered freely and without pressure or coercion, direct or implied, from an employer." A second is whether the work is the same type of work the individual is otherwise employed, for pay, to perform for the same organization; the same regulations state that "[a]n individual shall not be considered a volunteer if the individual is otherwise employed by the same public agency to perform the same type of services as those for which the individual proposes to volunteer." The Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division Field Operations Handbook applies a similar concept outside the public-agency context, stating, in discussing volunteers at religious, charitable, and nonprofit organizations, that "this does not mean that a regular office employee of a charitable organization can volunteer services on an uncompensated basis to handle correspondence in connection with a special fund drive or to handle other work arising from exigencies of the operations conducted by the employer" — meaning an employee's after-hours help in a different capacity may be genuine volunteering, while donating unpaid time to do more of the person's own paid job typically is not.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Congress did not intend to discourage or impede volunteer activities undertaken for civic, charitable, or humanitarian purposes, but expressed its wish to prevent any manipulation or abuse of minimum wage or overtime requirements through coercion or undue pressure upon individuals to “volunteer” their services."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 553.101(b) (Cornell LII text), Code of Federal Regulations, "volunteer" definition, statement of congressional intent (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/553.101)
  "Individuals shall be considered volunteers only where their services are offered freely and without pressure or coercion, direct or implied, from an employer."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 553.101(c) (Cornell LII text), Code of Federal Regulations, "volunteer" definition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/553.101)
  "An individual shall not be considered a volunteer if the individual is otherwise employed by the same public agency to perform the same type of services as those for which the individual proposes to volunteer."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 553.101(d) (Cornell LII text), Code of Federal Regulations, "volunteer" definition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/553.101)
  "this does not mean that a regular office employee of a charitable organization can volunteer services on an uncompensated basis to handle correspondence in connection with a special fund drive or to handle other work arising from exigencies of the operations conducted by the employer"
  — U.S. Dep't of Labor, Wage and Hour Division, Field Operations Handbook, Ch. 10, § 10b03 (current text, revision noted 03/31/2016), U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division, Field Operations Handbook (https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/WHD/legacy/files/FOH_Ch10.pdf)
  Known gap: The "offered freely and without coercion" and "not the same type of services" language quoted here from 29 C.F.R. § 553.101 comes from a regulation that, by its own terms, governs volunteers at public agencies, not private or nonprofit employers; this document could not verify that an identically worded regulation applies by its own terms outside that context, and presents these considerations as ones DOL sub-regulatory guidance (the Field Operations Handbook) and the same underlying policy concern apply by analogy in the private and nonprofit context, not as a codified private-sector test carrying the same regulatory force. This document does not itself weigh these considerations for any specific arrangement.

FOR-PROFIT EMPLOYERS AND VOLUNTEER STATUS
Department of Labor guidance draws a sharper line between nonprofit and for-profit employers than is sometimes assumed. The Department's own published FLSA Advisor states plainly: "Under the FLSA, employees may not volunteer services to for-profit private sector employers," while noting that, by contrast, "in the vast majority of circumstances, individuals can volunteer services to public sector employers." The same DOL guidance describes the volunteer doctrine discussed elsewhere in this document as applying to individuals who donate their services "usually on a part-time basis, for public service, religious or humanitarian objectives, not as employees and without contemplation of pay," and states that such individuals "are not considered employees of the religious, charitable or similar non-profit organizations that receive their service" — language limited to nonprofit organizations receiving the service, not ordinary for-profit businesses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Under the FLSA, employees may not volunteer services to for-profit private sector employers."
  — U.S. Dep't of Labor, elaws Fair Labor Standards Act Advisor, "Volunteers" (current text), U.S. Department of Labor, elaws FLSA Advisor (https://webapps.dol.gov/elaws/whd/flsa/docs/volunteers.asp)
  "Individuals who volunteer or donate their services, usually on a part-time basis, for public service, religious or humanitarian objectives, not as employees and without contemplation of pay, are not considered employees of the religious, charitable or similar non-profit organizations that receive their service."
  — U.S. Dep't of Labor, elaws Fair Labor Standards Act Advisor, "Volunteers" (current text), U.S. Department of Labor, elaws FLSA Advisor (https://webapps.dol.gov/elaws/whd/flsa/docs/volunteers.asp)
  Known gap: This is sub-regulatory DOL informal guidance (an elaws Advisor page), not a statute or regulation, and this document did not locate a court decision squarely addressing whether an individual could ever be found a bona fide unpaid volunteer at a for-profit employer under some other doctrine. An unpaid worker at a for-profit company is more likely to be analyzed under this corpus's separate discussion of unpaid interns and trainees than treated as a "volunteer" in the sense this document otherwise addresses; this document does not itself determine whether any specific for-profit arrangement is lawful.

A CHARITABLE PURPOSE ALONE DOES NOT CREATE VOLUNTEER STATUS
A nonprofit organization is not categorically exempt from the FLSA merely because of its charitable purpose — a point this corpus also makes in its separate discussion of unpaid internships — and the same is true specifically for people an organization calls "volunteers." In a 2023 decision, the Fifth Circuit affirmed a district court's application of the Supreme Court's "economic reality" test to unpaid participants in a nonprofit drug-and-alcohol rehabilitation program's work program, holding that the district court's "threshold determination that the rehabilitation patients constitute 'employees' under the Act because they worked in expectation of compensation was not an abuse of discretion." The court also rejected the argument that the organization's own paperwork could settle the question: although participants had signed forms stating they were "beneficiaries," not employees, the court held that "any forms patients sign indicating that they are beneficiaries and not employees do not control this analysis," because rights under the FLSA cannot be waived by agreement. In other words, what an organization calls an unpaid worker, or what that worker agrees to be called, does not itself determine status under the Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Its threshold determination that the rehabilitation patients constitute “employees” under the Act because they worked in expectation of compensation was not an abuse of discretion."
  — Klick v. Cenikor Foundation (CourtListener text), 79 F.4th 433 (5th Cir. 2023) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9420693/klick-v-cenikor-foundation/)
  "any forms patients sign indicating that they are beneficiaries and not employees do not control this analysis."
  — Klick v. Cenikor Foundation (CourtListener text), 79 F.4th 433 (5th Cir. 2023) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9420693/klick-v-cenikor-foundation/)
  Known gap: This Fifth Circuit decision resolved an interlocutory appeal about whether a collective action could be certified and whether the district court used the correct legal framework — it did not itself finally decide, on the merits, that the rehabilitation program's participants were employees; that question was left for further proceedings. This document does not restate the separate primary-beneficiary internship test or the Tony and Susan Alamo Foundation Supreme Court decision discussed in this corpus's Unpaid Internship Compliance Information Sheet, which it treats as a related but distinct topic rather than duplicating here. This document does not itself determine that any specific nonprofit's unpaid workers are, or are not, employees under the Act.

CALIFORNIA SUBSTANTIALLY FOLLOWS THE FEDERAL VOLUNTEER FRAMEWORK
California's Labor Code and the Industrial Welfare Commission's Wage Orders do not set out a separate statutory or regulatory definition of "volunteer" distinct from the federal approach described elsewhere in this document. California's Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (DLSE), in its own currently published Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, addresses unpaid workers at nonprofit organizations by stating that a person who donates services to a religious, charitable, or similar nonprofit corporation, acting "without contemplation of pay and for public service, religious, or humanitarian objectives, are not employees" — a standard the manual attributes to a 1988 DLSE opinion letter, not to any specific Labor Code section or Wage Order provision addressing volunteers. As with the federal DOL guidance discussed elsewhere in this document, this DLSE position is limited to religious, charitable, or similar nonprofit corporations; it does not, by its own terms, extend to for-profit businesses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "without contemplation of pay and for public service, religious, or humanitarian objectives, are not employees."
  — California DLSE, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 43.6.7, "Volunteers" (current California Department of Industrial Relations text), California Department of Industrial Relations, Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dlse/DLSEManual/dlse_enfcmanual.pdf)
  Known gap: This document located no separate California statute or regulation defining "volunteer" for wage-and-hour purposes distinct from this DLSE guidance. The DLSE manual attributes this specific position to a 1988 opinion letter without a more recent restatement on this point, so this document cannot rule out that DLSE's position has evolved since 1988 in ways this publicly posted manual excerpt does not reflect; this document fetched the manual live from California's Department of Industrial Relations website on the date shown above and quotes it as currently published there. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine that any specific California unpaid arrangement is, or is not, a lawful volunteer relationship.

NOMINAL FEES, BENEFITS, AND EXPENSE REIMBURSEMENT FOR VOLUNTEERS
Federal regulations addressing volunteers who serve public agencies provide that "[v]olunteers may be paid expenses, reasonable benefits, a nominal fee, or any combination thereof, for their service without losing their status as volunteers," and separately specify that "[a] nominal fee is not a substitute for compensation and must not be tied to productivity." These regulations decline to set a fixed dollar figure for what counts as "nominal." Instead, they state that "[w]hether the furnishing of expenses, benefits, or fees would result in individuals' losing their status as volunteers under the FLSA can only be determined by examining the total amount of payments made (expenses, benefits, fees) in the context of the economic realities of the particular situation" — a fact-specific inquiry that also considers factors such as the distance traveled, the time and effort expended, and whether the individual is available around-the-clock or only periodically.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Volunteers may be paid expenses, reasonable benefits, a nominal fee, or any combination thereof, for their service without losing their status as volunteers."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 553.106(a) (Cornell LII text), Code of Federal Regulations, payment of expenses, benefits, or fees to volunteers (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/553.106)
  "A nominal fee is not a substitute for compensation and must not be tied to productivity."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 553.106(e) (Cornell LII text), Code of Federal Regulations, payment of expenses, benefits, or fees to volunteers (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/553.106)
  "Whether the furnishing of expenses, benefits, or fees would result in individuals' losing their status as volunteers under the FLSA can only be determined by examining the total amount of payments made (expenses, benefits, fees) in the context of the economic realities of the particular situation."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 553.106(f) (Cornell LII text), Code of Federal Regulations, payment of expenses, benefits, or fees to volunteers (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/553.106)
  Known gap: These regulations, by their own terms (29 C.F.R. Part 553), govern volunteers at public agencies — state and local governments — not private employers, whether nonprofit or for-profit. This document did not locate a Department of Labor regulation of equivalent specificity addressing what expense reimbursement, benefits, or nominal fees a private-sector or nonprofit volunteer may receive without losing volunteer status, and did not verify whether, or to what extent, courts or DOL guidance apply this public-agency "nominal fee" framework by analogy outside the public-agency context. This is accordingly presented as an unsettled, fact-specific area for private-sector and nonprofit volunteers rather than one governed by a confirmed bright-line rule; this document does not itself determine whether any particular payment or benefit is "nominal."

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan Lee and Acme Charitable Foundation each acknowledge that they have reviewed the volunteer role declaration above and this information sheet's description of the federal and California legal standards that can apply to unpaid volunteer arrangements.

Executed on October 1, 2026 at San Francisco, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

Signature on behalf of Acme Charitable Foundation: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes the FLSA's "employ" definition, the judicially recognized volunteer exception, federal regulations addressing public-agency volunteers, Department of Labor guidance addressing private-sector and nonprofit volunteers, and California's DLSE guidance on this topic. It is not a legal opinion about Jordan Lee's status, does not itself determine that this arrangement is, or is not, lawfully unpaid under the Fair Labor Standards Act or California law, is not a substitute for the statutes, regulations, and case law it describes, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.]

citations.quote: Whether the furnishing of expenses, benefits, or fees would result in individuals' losing their status as volunteers under the FLSA can only be determined by examining the total amount of payments made (expenses, benefits, fees) in the context of the economic realities of the particular situation.

expectedJSON.gap: These regulations, by their own terms (29 C.F.R. Part 553), govern volunteers at public agencies — state and local governments — not private employers, whether nonprofit or for-profit. This document did not locate a Department of Labor regulation of equivalent specificity addressing what expense reimbursement, benefits, or nominal fees a private-sector or nonprofit volunteer may receive without losing volunteer status, and did not verify whether, or to what extent, courts or DOL guidance apply this public-agency "nominal fee" framework by analogy outside the public-agency context. This is accordingly presented as an unsettled, fact-specific area for private-sector and nonprofit volunteers rather than one governed by a confirmed bright-line rule; this document does not itself determine whether any particular payment or benefit is "nominal."

[This information sheet describes the FLSA's "employ" definition, the judicially recognized volunteer exception, federal regulations addressing public-agency volunteers, Department of Labor guidance addressing private-sector and nonprofit volunteers, and California's DLSE guidance on this topic. It is not a legal opinion about Jordan Lee's status, does not itself determine that this arrangement is, or is not, lawfully unpaid under the Fair Labor Standards Act or California law, is not a substitute for the statutes, regulations, and case law it describes, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.]
